what: The Problem: Sampling Bias in Data-Poor Regions
title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: building Species Distribution Models (SDMs), researchers need “background” points represent available environment. data-rich regions, “target-group backgrounds” used cancel sampling bias. However, data-poor regions (like many parts Global South), target-group data exist. Randomly sampling background points causes model learn “roads ” rather “species lives.”

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: biasProxyR solves using open-source infrastructure data (like OpenStreetMap road networks) create “Sampling Effort Proxy” surface. allows researchers sample background points mathematically match geographic bias occurrence data.

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: First, generate sampling effort proxy country. tutorial, use Luxembourg small processes quickly. ``{r generate-effort, message=TRUE, cache=TRUE} # Generate 1000m resolution effort surface Luxembourg effort <- generate_effort_surface(“Luxembourg”, resolution = 1000)

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: terra::plot(effort, main = “Sampling Effort Proxy - Luxembourg”, col = terrain.colors(50))
code: *Brighter areas indicate higher probability of human sampling effort (e.g., near cities and major highways).*  ## Step 2: Sample Bias-Aware Background Points  Instead of sampling background points randomly, we use the effort surface to weight our sampling. This ensures our background points have the same geographic bias as typical GBIF occurrence data.  ```{r sample-bg, message=TRUE, cache=TRUE}` # Sample 2,000 bias-aware background points bg_points <- sample_bias_aware_background(effort, n_points = 2000)  # Plot the points over the effort surface terra::plot(effort, main = "Bias-Aware Background Points", col = terrain.colors(50)) plot(bg_points, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: already occurrence data, can use diagnostic tool see biased even run SDM. ``{r diagnose, message=TRUE, cache=TRUE} # Run diagnostic sampled points (pretending occurrence data) diagnostic_results <- diagnose_sampling_bias(bg_points, effort)

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: print(diagnostic_results$bias_score_percent) ```

title: Getting Started with biasProxyR
text: Now bias-aware background points, can feed directly favorite SDM package (like maxnet, biomod2, sdm) alongside true presence data build ecologically realistic models!

title: Sampling Effort Proxies for Species Distribution Models
text: building Species Distribution Models (SDMs) like MaxNet Random Forest, researchers need “background” points represent available environment. Global North, researchers often use “target-group backgrounds” cancel sampling bias. Global South (e.g., Pakistan, Brazil, Kenya), target-group backgrounds often exist baseline biodiversity data sparse. sample background points randomly across country, model doesn’t learn species grows; just learns “roads cities .” example, Pakistan, approximately 75% GBIF plant records concentrated single province (Punjab), leaving entire regions like Balochistan “data deserts.” Standard SDM workflows fail account severe geographic bias.

title: Sampling Effort Proxies for Species Distribution Models
text: biasProxyR uses freely available global remote sensing infrastructure data map “probability human sampling effort.” Researchers can use proxy map intelligently sample background points match bias occurrence data, statistically correct way handle sampling bias target-group data absent.

title: Sampling Effort Proxies for Species Distribution Models
text: generate_effort_surface(): Downloads road density data given country combines single raster representing probability human sampling effort. sample_bias_aware_background(): Samples background points SDMs proportionally effort surface, effectively canceling geographic bias data-poor regions. diagnose_sampling_bias(): publication-ready diagnostic tool plots occurrence points effort surface calculates “Bias Correlation Score” warn users severe sampling skew.
